title: Detection of Gather Victim Host Information
shortTitle: Detection of Gather Victim Host Information
summary: This strategy detects Gather Victim Host Information, the reconnaissance step in which an adversary learns the hardware, software, and configuration of hosts in your environment. It matters because that inventory shapes everything that follows: the tooling they bring, the vulnerabilities they try, and the phishing lures they write. Detection depends on joining endpoint inventory queries, directory LDAP searches for computer objects, and external vulnerability or port scan telemetry, then correlating them by source. The usual failure mode is volume: legitimate asset management, patch, and inventory tools touch the same systems constantly, so the value comes from comparing a source against its own baseline rather than from a single event.

beginner.definition: This detection watches for signs that someone is learning about the computers in your network. It catches activity that collects details such as operating system, installed software, open ports, and hardware type. The aim is to spot the study phase that comes before an attack.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attacker who knows your systems can pick the right tools and the right weakness. That makes the later attack faster and more likely to work. Many teams only watch for the break in, not the study before it. Catching this early gives you time to block the source. It also tells you which systems an intruder already cares about.
howItWorks: Endpoint and inventory tools record each time a program lists installed software or system details.
A central log, such as a security information and event management system, collects those records.
The rule looks for many inventory style lookups from one account or one host in a short time.
It also adds records of port scans and directory computer searches that come from the same source.
Analysts compare the source with a list of approved scanners and inventory servers.
If the source is not approved, the system raises an alert for a person to review.
beginner.example: Think of a night watchman in a large office building. Before a burglary, someone often walks the halls and notes which doors are unlocked and which windows are old. The watchman alone cannot arrest anyone, but the walking pattern is a clear clue. In the same way, an odd burst of inventory lookups is not an attack by itself, but it tells you that someone is mapping your building.
takeaways: Host information gathering is the study step that comes before an attack.
The same tools your own team uses create the same pattern, so approved sources must be filtered out.
Correlating the source across endpoint, directory, and network logs turns weak signals into a useful one.

objectives: Explain why host information gathering is treated as a detectable step before exploitation
Identify the telemetry sources that record system, software, and port discovery activity
Correlate an inventory query with a later scan from the same source address or account
Build an allow list of approved inventory and scanning hosts to reduce false alerts
Recognise the point at which reconnaissance becomes preparation for a specific attack
dataSources: Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing enabled, showing systeminfo, wmic, or net commands
Sysmon event 1 process creation including parent image and command line for host discovery utilities
Active Directory LDAP diagnostic logging of searches for computer and operating system attributes
Firewall and intrusion detection system logs of port sweep attempts against internal host ranges
Inventory or endpoint management agent audit logs listing installed software and hardware queries
logic: The pattern is a burst of host description activity: command lines that read operating system and hardware details, directory searches that return computer objects in bulk, and port sweeps against internal address ranges. Correlating the user, the source host, and the network address shows whether the requests come from one actor or many. Benign cases come from approved inventory servers, patch tools, and security scanners that run on a schedule and repeat the same behaviour every day. The malicious case is a new or unusual source performing the same reads, often spread across unrelated subnets and timed just before another suspicious event.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Host Information Gathering Burst
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: security
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventID: 4688
#     CommandLine|contains:
#       - 'systeminfo'
#       - 'wmic'
#       - 'Get-CimInstance Win32_'
#   filter:
#     User|endswith: '$'
#     ParentImage|contains: 'InventoryServer'
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: medium
falsePositives: Asset inventory and configuration management agents that enumerate installed software on a fixed schedule
Patch management servers that query operating system build and hotfix levels across the estate
Help desk engineers running systeminfo or wmic during a troubleshooting call
Approved vulnerability scanners performing authenticated host enumeration from a known scanner address
tuningNotes: Start by baselining which accounts and hosts normally run host discovery commands, then scope the rule to production subnets where such queries are rare and keep separate handling for the IT management VLAN where they are expected. Filter machine accounts ending in a dollar sign, approved scanner network ranges, and scheduled task parents. Build the allow list from observed inventory before enabling alerts, and review it quarterly. Narrowing cuts noise but you lose coverage of an intruder who lands on a management host, so keep a low severity version of the rule running estate-wide for hunting.
